maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I would say that before we proceed with this Bill the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) promised to bring down the recommendations made by certain persons outside, and any expressions of opinion received in regard to it. The hon. gentleman has not been good enough to favour us with those yet.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I think that what my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) alludes to is the way in which this Bill was distributed amongst the people to give them an opportunity of studying it during the last recess and also an epitome of the expressions of opinion received from the people to whom this Bill was sent. I have here in my hand a statement of the distribution as made of 32,000 copies of this Bill. We sent out the Bill for the purpose of eliciting an expression of opinion from the people who are interested in it, in the following way :	To
seed merchants in Canada, wholesale and retail 6.500 copies, to all the members of the Dominion Seed Growers' Association 430

copies, to all tlie officers of the different farmers' institutes, agricultural societies and farmers' clubs in all of the provinces, 6,340 copies, to newspapers in all provinces together with newspaper bulletin 970 copies, to members of parliament 210 copies, exchange list, that is experimental stations abroad, 230 copies, to individual applicants 550 copies, per department farmers' mailing list and to lists of members of agricultural organizations whose names were in the department, about 15,500 copies, in store about 1,270 at the date this memorandum was made out. I might in explanation, say that arrangements were made with the superintendents of the farmers' institutes in each of the provinces so that one man on each deputation or delegation was instructed to discuss the subject at every meeting. They wmre provided from the office of the seed division here with printed charts, with samples of various seeds and summary information showing the results of the investigations in the seed laboratory of the department here. There were about 900 of these farmers' meetings held. We have no absolute definite information that this Bill was read and discussed at all of them, but the reports that have been received from the institute lecturers would indicate that it was discussed at all of them, and that there is a strong desire on the part of the farmers in Canada for an Act that will tend to suppress the evils connected with the seed trade. Twenty-seven of these reports have been received from agricultural lecturers each of whom spoke at a large number of meetings and they all clearly show that the provisions of the Bill were fully supported by the farmers at every meeting. The only suggestions that have been made by farmers were to the effect that the Bill should be made more stringent. A large number of letters commenting on the Bill have been received from individual farmers during the past two months, and in all of them there has been an urgent appeal for the passage of this Bill and asking that it shall be made law without any unnecessary delay. I may say further that no communication has been received from any farmer entering any protest at all, or in any way pointing out that the provisions of the Bill would hamper his operations. We have received communications from some 13 seedsmen, more than one letter from many of them. In some of these the provisions of the Bill were pointed out as being too stringent. Several of the seedsmen considered that having to label all packages of timothy, alsike and red clover seed would greatly hamper them in carrying on their business. Letters were received from two seed merchants in support of the Bill as it now stands. We received a number of resolutions that were passed by the following- organizations :	The Farmers' and
Dairymen's Association of New Brunswick, on February 23, 1903; the Nova Scotia Farmers' Association on February 9, 1903 ;
the Ontario Agricultural and Experimental Union on February 5, 1904 ; South Renfrew Farmers' Institute at meetings held at Brudenell, ICillaloe, Stewartville, Loch Win-noch, White Lake, Burnston, Gratton, Mount St. Patrick, Shamrock and Renfrew, on February 27, 1904 ; the Central Farmers' Institute for British Columbia on April 27, 1904 ; the South Brant Farmers' Institute ; resolutions adopted at different meetings held in the riding, February 29, 1904 ; the East Peterboro' Farmers' Institute on December 5, 190.3 ; the Metchosen Farmers' the Farmer' Institute convention held at Indian Head, Assiniboia, Feb. 11, 1904 ; the Farmers' Institute convention held at Brandon, February 10, 1904, and Farmers' Institute meetings in Haldimand, Monck, Brant, Oxford and Norfolk, 33 meetings in all where after discussion, votes on this question were taken and resolutions passed. I am informed that there was no opposition to these votes.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman the resolutions that were passed, and can he tell the committee whether these Farmers' Institutes propose to adopt the hon. gentleman's Bill or a Bill in this direction ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: We received a good many of these resolutions from the officers of these institutes, though not all of them. We also have letters from several others of the Farmers' Institute, lecturers who state in general terms that a large number of resolutions favouring the Bill have been passed by a number of local Farmers' Institutes. In these cases particulars have not been received by the department. The council of the corporation of Matsqui, British Columbia, have also passed a resolution. While I am on my feet, perhaps I may say a few words in general terms upon this Bill.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
Before the hon. gentleman proceeds to explain, I would like to say that I must confess that I am somewhat disappointed at the information the hon. gentleman has given us. I am thoroughly in sympathy with a measure in the direction in which this Bill goes, but it was rather a surprise to the committee, I am sure, to me to learn that the hon. gentleman has received no support generally for his Bill, as it is, from localities in Canada the least interested in many features of this Bill. I would like to know, to what very great extent the maritime provinces and the western provinces are interested in the cultivation of clover for instance. I am surprised to find that the Bill has been so little endorsed generally throughout the country. We all know that when resolutions are passed at these meetings in favour of a Bill, such resolutions refer to the provisions of the Bill generally, and not to its details. I think there should have been more general ap-

proval before the Bill was presented to the House.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: There were in all thirty-three farmers' institute meetings.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: How many of these passed resolutions ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: A vote was taken in all of these, and there was no dissentient vote. These meetings were held in Haldimand, Monk, Brant, Oxford and Norfolk; some of them large seed-growing counties in the province of Ontario.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to read one of these reso lutions.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: And at the same time state how many persons were present at each of these meetings ; as a rule there are about half a dozen.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
This is a specimen resolution -which was sent from Burford, Ont., and it is written by I. T. Taylor, secretary of the South Brant Farmers' Institute, and addressed to myself :
Feb. 29, 1904.
Dear Sir,-At a series of Farmers' Institute meetings held in South Brant during this month, the subject of good seeds, and weeds was discussed, and the Bill called the Seeds Control Act introduced by yourself at the last session of parliament, was brought before the farmers and discussed. The following resolution was adopted at seven different meetings in the riding, and I was instructed to forward a copy to you :-
Resolved (re Seeds Control Act), moved by Thomas Parkes and seconded by Owen McAlister, that we, the members of the South Brant Farmers' Institute having been made acquainted with the provisions of the Seeds Control Act which was introduced in the House of Commons last session and laid over on account of opposition from seed merchants and other, and for non-support by those directly interested, desire to express our hearty approval of the said Act, believing that it would be in the direct interest of the farmers of the Dominion if such a law were placed on the statute-books, and that a copy of this be sent to our representative and also to the hon. Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: That looks like a stereotyped- resolution prepared and carried around.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I have no means of knowing anything of the kind ; it was not prepared and it was not stereotyped by any body in connection with my department. My statement is, I think, correct, that this Bill was discussed at several hundred farmers' gatherings of one kind or another since last session of parliament, and the opinion of the farmers expressed at these meetings was practically unanimously in favour of it. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) himself says that he is in sympathy with the Mr. CLANCY.
principle of the Bill. There are several interests in the country which are affected more or less by this Bill; there are the farmers who buy the seeds ; there are the men who deal in these seeds, retail and wholesale, and there are the producers of the seeds. The origin of this Bill was a feeling amongst the farmers that they had no means to protect themselves against paying for bad seed, and against the even far greater injury fo them of sowing weed seeds instead of genuine seeds. This feeling was most insistent amongst the farmers of Quebec and the maritime provinces, who have suffered more than the farmers of the great province of Ontario in this respect.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Where did these bad seeds come from ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: It is rather difficult to trace where they come from, but of course they are sold to the farmers by dealers. In the maritime provinces hardly any seed is raised for sale ; in Quebec a certain amount is raised for sale in a few localities, but the great bulk of the seed raised for sale in Canada comes from the province of Ontario. Most of that seed is raised in perfect good faith by the men who raise it. They raise it to the best of their ability under their present conditions and methods, for the purpose of selling it in a legitimate way. As a matter of fact, everybody knows, nobody better than the seed merchants who purchase it, that a great deal of that seed is not of first quality, but is mixed with weeds or other seeds, while a good deal is not well ripened and consequently is not germinal. I do not say this as any reflection on the men who raise the seeds. They have been carrying on this business for many years to the. best of their ability and in a practical way; but at the same time the results have not been what the purchasers of the seed had a right to expect.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that farmers generally have not in their minds the idea that the grain or seed they are growing is to be used as seed. Does the hon. gentleman mean the farmers or the seed growers, and to a large extent the seed merchants ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I was speaking more particularly of small seeds like the seeds of grasses and clovers. Seed grain is raised very frequently without any intention of it being sold for seed purposes.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: So is clover.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Sometimes clover is, although I am in the judgment of those who know the business when I say that in most cases it is grown for the purpose of being sold as seed.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: That is my opinion. The hon. gentleman may be right and I may be wrong.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: In the locality where a great quantity of clover seed is grown I know that is not the case. Much of it is for export.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to say that it is grown for export, and not to be sold in Canada ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Not especially. It is not grown to be sold as seed.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I cannot accept that statement altogether. The man who raises clover seed, speaking of the large farmers, would probably at the outside require for himself a few hundred pounds, and he might very easily have a thousand pounds or more, perhaps several thousand pounds, and he certainly would not be cutting and thrashing all that and making it into seed for his own use alone. He would use as much as he wanted for himself, but a great deal of it would be sold. As a matter of fact, we know that in certain sections of the province of Ontario men raise large quantities of clover and grass seed for sale. Those men have been carrying on the business, I believe, to the best of their ability ; but old, cultivated land is frequently found to produce other seeds and weed seeds. The result is that a very large portion of the seed bought by the seed merchants has not been thoroughly cleaned before being put on the market, and is not of a quality which the purchaser would wish to take. Of the three classes chiefly interested in this business, we have first the producers, next those who buy the seeds from the farmers, the merchants, who clean the seeds and sell them again to farmers, retail merchants and jobbers. There are a number of great com-, mercial houses in Canada engaged in this business. I think the great majority of them do their business excellently well. They do the necessary cleaning of the seeds. They have special machinery and appliances for the purpose. They sell to the local dealers, and these in turn sell to the farmers. My object in drawing this Bill, and in all these investigations and discussions which have preceded it, has been to try to secure for the farmers of the country as pure and good seeds as it is possible to get for them, keeping clearly in mind the necessities of the business in all its branches-to interfere just as little as possible with the course of this business and with the people engaged in it. I wish to avoid as much as possible interference with the ordinary channels of trade or the practices followed, except when those practices are not in the interest of the community. I want to state very emphatically that I do not think there has been intentional fraud on the part of those engaged in the seed trade in Canada. The men who grow seed grain and clean it necessarily 157
obtain in that process different grades. They have the very best seed, that which is practically absolutely pure and germinal. Some merchants adopt standards, differing from others. Some divide their seeds into a greater or lesser number of grades and sell the seed according to its grade. The majority of farmers, I think, do not appreciate or understand the great difference there is in the purity and cleanliness of the different grades of seed. The result has been that a great many people, I will not say were intentionally inclined to be fraudulent, but as a matter of fact were selling to the farmers of the country grades of seeds which the producer, if he knew their quality, would not have thought of buying at the prices which he paid for them.	.
This condition of affairs is what justifies the passage of such an Act. It is impossible for the ordinary purchaser to be able to know that he is getting exactly the seeds he intended buying. In some things a man can judge what he is getting. If he buys a horse he can examine it and tell in a general way what it is worth. But the ordinary farmer, when he buys seeds, cannot tell whether he is getting good value, because in order to do so he would have to examine them under a microscope or powerful magnifying glass. He would require to know also the different varieties of seeds, and this therefore seems to me a legitimate case for the passing of a law to regulate transactions of this kind. After careful consideration of the question I brought in an Act last session, but the seed merchants think that its provisions are too stringent and have found that they could not carry on their business under it. I have therefore in the present Bill considerably modified the' provisions of the Act in the direction desired by those engaged in the trade. 1 have not however gone quite as far as the seed merchants asked, for if I had, I would not be able to protect the purchasers. This subject is one of great importance to agriculturists' and I am quite willing to adopt any suggestions which may make the law more workable and effective.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
'I am afraid that the hon. gentleman will not find that support for his Bill from public opinion which is necessary in order to make any law effective. The question has not been presented to our farmers in such a way that they could have an opportunity of giving their views upon it, but has simply been presented at institute meetings by men whose object was not to have the defects of the measure discussed but to have it extolled as something which could not fail to* benefit the farmers. And the only support he has been able to secure for his Bill in its details is one which he took care to secure. All he has been able to produce is a copy of a resolution passed at an institute meeting in this province, but any one knows how easy it is



to secure an endorsation of tliat kind. I happened to be present at one of those meetings and I found that the farmers, instead of being invited to discuss the measure, were simply treated to an elaborate panegyric of it. Let me refer to the very first clause :
No person shall sell

That prohibition applies to every man, whether he grows seed for himself upon his twenty-five acre farm or whether he is a large farmer or a dealer in seed, who may be buying and selling in the ordinary way.
No person shall sell or expose or have in his possession for sale for the purpose of seeding

How is the minister going to determine whether a farmer has seed in his possession for the purpose of seeding or not? The thing is abolutely unworkable. Every one does -not grow seed to sell as seed and, though the Minister of Agriculture may say that the Bill is adapted to the conditions, yet, without presuming to contradict the hon. gentleman, I may be. allowed to humbly suggest that that does not settle the question- it is not proof. I venture so far as to tell the hon. gentleman that his Bill is based upon wrong principles, that is upon principles that cannot be reduced to practice in this everyday world. If the hon. gentleman wished to provide against seed merchants willingly, knowingly, allowing seed to leave their warehouses in utter disregard of its composition, that might be a very proper measure. My experience small as it has been, I think, is a fair guide to the actual conditions. I believe We have very few seedsmen in Canada who will knowingly send out bad seed. It is to the interest of every reputable seed merchant-I am speaking more particularly of the province of Ontario-to be most careful about the kind of seed he sends out because his house may be brought into disrepute in a single day if the seed he sells is other than he represents it to be. He can only hope to gain and keep the support of men by being careful and reliable. The hon. minister has not said that in the province of Ontario there has been any widespread complaint on that ground. I have not heard of a single case of any reputable seed house in Ontario sending out a pound of bad seed. If there is a general outcry on that ground, I confess I have not heard it ; and if there has not been a general outcry, I would ask the hon. minister from what quarter comes the demand for this Bill, this mischievous Bill so far as appears on the face of it, which is now introduced for thu second time ? The hon. minister must have had something to warrant him in introducing so drastic a measure. He must have information to show that, the farmers have been made, Intentionally or unintentionally, the victims of bad seed. If there is any complaint in the pro-Mr. CLANCY.
vince of Ontario perhaps he will givp me some evidence of it.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
Let me deal in order witli the two points the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy has raised. In the first place, speaking of the resolution which I read, he seemed to think it was a resolution that had been put before a lot of farmers' institutes and passed in stereotyped form. In answer, I may tell the hon. gentleman that no such resolution was prepared by anybody that I know of. The meetings were left entirely to themselves as to the form of the resolution and as to whether they would pass resolutions or not, or give any expression of opinion. I will read one or two resolutions to show that the form was not stereotyped. Here is another which reached me from German, and was the expression of opinion from the Farmers' Institute of East Peterborough :
Resolved, that in the opinion of the Farmers' Institute of East Peterborough the Bill respecting the inspection of seeds offered for sale is a step in the right direction, and the government will have the hearty support of this institute when considering this Bill.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Does this refer to the Bill of this year or of last year ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: To the Bill of last year which was a more stringent Bill.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I know it was. Last year's Bill was an impossibility.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
And yet, this farmers' institute said that we should have their hearty support in considering that Bill. I have another resolution here, but I see that it comes from Midland, New Brunswick. As my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) speaks especially of Ontario I can hardly read this to prove to my hou. friend anything about Ontario, but the form of it will show that the resolution is not stereotyped :
Moved by F. E. Sharp, seconded by W. W. Fawcett and resolved : Having had the results of this work given to us to-day and knowing that the conditions referred to are common to the whole Dominion, this convention of the New Brunswick Farmers' and Dairymen's Association

This, it seems, was the provincial association, and not simply a local institute.
-urge upon the minister the necessity for immediate legislation which shall fix proper standards of grading with respect to the purity and vitality of seeds of grasses and clover, and shall establish a system of official control to prevent imposition upon the farmers by such regulation? and penalties as will ensure its observance.
And this is the letter accompanying the resolution. It is dated from Chatham, New Brunswick and signed A. G. Dixon :
I beg leave to submit for your consideration tile inclosed resolution, which passed unanimously at our annual convention held recently

at Sussex, N.B. This resolution seemed to express the sentiment of 300 farmers present. If such legislation should be obtained and the observance of such law carried out, it would save the farmers from being imposed upon by unreliable seedsmen and dealers from which they have suffered such a loss in the past.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Where are the resolutions from Ontario, the seed growing province 1

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I have one here from the south riding of Renfrew.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Of course, we know what that is in advance.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: It will be all right.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) does not need to believe anything he does not wish to. But this is a resolution from Ontario, and my hon. friend should take that for gospel. The letter accompanying the resolution is as follows :
At the several meetings held during the past winter in Brudenell, Killaloe, Stewart-ville, Loch Winnoch, White Lake, Burnstown, Grattan, Mt. St. Patrick, Shamrock and Renfrew, the inclosed resolution was presented and unanimously adopted, and consider it of the greatest importance that the farmers of this section should be able to secure seeds practically free from foul seeds.
This is signed by Gregor MacIntyre, secretary South Renfrew Farmers' Institute. And this is the resolution :
Whereas, at the various branch farmers' institute meetings held in the south riding of Renfrew during the present winter the matter of having such a Bill passed by the House of Commons as was introduced last session by the Hon. Sydney Fisher, whereby some guarantee will be given to farmers, who of necessity must buy a large amount of seed each year, that he is getting clean and fertile seeds.
And whereas, at all these branch meetings the members have either by resolution or otherwise, expressed their unqualified approval of having such an Act passed.
It is resolved by the members of this Central Farmers' Institute, that we heartily approve of the efforts now being put forth in this direction and the members of this institute desire that our secretary be and hereby is requested to notify our representative in the House of Commons of the action that has been taken by tbe various branch institutes of the riding and to request that he use every legitimate means to assist in having such a measure become the law of the land.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I will leave that subject for the resolutions in favour of this measure. They all embody the idea that the farmers have a grievance, a difficulty in tlieir business, and they want to see that difficulty removed and their situation improved.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I sat down to give the hon. gentleman an opportunity to give some evidence of a popular demand for this Bill, some evidence of the difficulty, of the loT^
evil that induced the hon. gentleman to introduce this measure. The hon. gentleman has merely given us some advertisements of his measure. I would like him to tell us from what quarter the outcry lias come for a measure of this kind.
ilr. FISHER. I have not got that information under my hand to-day, because it was all produced last session. If the hon. gentleman will look up the debates of last session he will find the information I then gave to the committee, and which I will repeat before the Bill goes through if the hon. gentleman desires it. I think when the hon. gentleman opened his remarks this afternoon he stated that he believed in the principle of the Bill, believed. I thought (he said, that there was a necessity for some such a Bill.	.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
No.
Mr. FISHER, Then I understand that he does not believe in the necessitv of such a Bill ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think there is no necessity for legislation in regard to the business of seed distribution in this country?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I will say to the hon. gentleman that I think all questions of this nature should receive attention from time to time, but the legislation must be upon such grounds as will commend itself to the approval of the people, whether in that line or any other line. I am in sympathy with any measure that will correct such evils as can be corrected by law. I ask the hon. gentleman to point to one seed merchant in the province of Ontario who has been guilty, either by inadvertence, deliberation or disregard, of sending out bad seed to the farmers. There may be such cases but I am not aware of them ; but if there are, a remedy should be found, and a drastic remedy.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I have not yet heard the Minister of Agriculture produce any demands for the introduction of this Bill. But I understand that the Minister himself is a practical farmer, and if he is, he knows how much weeds cost the farmers of this country, and therefore he does not require any prompting, I should think, from other farmers. Besides, if he were not a farmer, he has only to travel on the railroad through the country to see what weeds are costing the farmers, what harm they are doing to the farms. If you travel over the railroads at the present moment you will see in many fields nothing but yellow mustard, and you will see in other fields nothing but white daisies. There are other weeds just as obnoxious. As has been said by my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. COMMONS
Clancy), I think this Bill is in the right direction. But it is a question with me whether it is not too drastic for the seedsman and farmers, even as it stands now. But we all know that we must place before us a high ideal in order to obtain fairly good ends. I had the pleasure of attending two farmers' institutes last winter, and one gentleman came there, a farmer I think, and he showed us a number of obnoxious weed seeds in different kinds of grain. In one pound of clover he said he had found over a thousand weed seeds.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: That is an extraordinary statement.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I am only giving his statement. I never counted them or measured them. However, I have no rea'son to doubt his word. We know that when a man grows seed he grows it for sale, he sells what he does not require to sow on his own ground, he does not grow seed to burn. His object is to make money out of it, and he could not make money if he destroyed it. Besides the seedsmen, the farmer also sells seed and gets as much money as he can for it. I think the seedsmen are in sympathy with this Bill, because they desire to buy pure seed. To my knowledge they have means of cleaning it up, they have got the machinery for cleaning nearly all the weed seeds out of the pure seed. Unless they do this there should be a law to make them do it. If this Bill is carried and put into force we will not see in every second field these obnoxious weeds. At present these weeds are a source of great loss to the farming community, and if the Minister of Agriculture can do anything to relieve the farmers of this heavy loss he will accomplish something very desirable. The object is to give the farmers pure seed and to induce the farmers to be sure and raise pure seed, but when the minister puts in this Bill, as I I see there is in one clause, a provision that 99 per cent of a quantity of seed must be pure and that 99 per cent of it must grow, then I think he is going a little too far because I am satisfied that no man can raise seed 99 per cent of which will grow, no matter how pure the seed may be. He ought to try and make this Bill workable, but I think it is going a little too far to oblige every seedsman and every second farmer to pay a heavy fine or serve one month in jail if he is found selling impure seed.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I think it would be desirable if the hon. minister would give us an explanation of the differences between the present Bill and the Bill he introduced last session. speechtext: If the evil was general would the farmers complain generally of that state of affairs ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Yes, I think they would. 1 think that what the hon. member for Elgin said a few minutes ago is perfectly true that one has only to go around the country to see what an immense number of weeds there are growing in our fields. The farmers want to get rid of these weeds. What I said before was that the farmers cannot detect these weed seeds in the seed which they buy themselves. It is practically impossible. A very clever well-informed and observant farmer can take a sample of seed in his hand and know only in a very general way whether it is fairly clean or not. That is about the extent he can go. But by a laboratory analysis you can get that information.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman received complaints from Ontario ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Not in the correspondence, but I may have general letters in the department. This question was dealt with last year. I have not with me to-day for the purpose of this discussion the information which I* gave to the House last year. I think that I did give to the House then considerable evidence of the fact that there was a general demand in this country for this legislation. Four or five years ago, when the work of the seed laboratory was first begun, there was comparatively little information of an exact character before the farmers of the country. But, they felt they were buying bad seed. I have had numerous conversations with farmers and 1 have had complaints of various kinds with regard to seeds but at the same time until the seed laboratory was established and until analyses were made of seeds, the information which is given in this bulletin was not available to farmers. When they got that information I venture to say that a great many farmers were startled and taken aback and felt that something must be done to save their farms from this evil. They knew the evil existed but they did not know to what extent it existed, they had no details or information upon which they could found any charge or argument and the seed laboratory has supplied that to a considerable extent.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
It strikes me as a remarkable state of affairs. I hold in my hand the report of the Bureau of Industries for Ontario for 1902, and I will point out to the hon. gentleman that on pages 8 and 9 it deals with fall wheat, spring wheat and barley, and on the following page with oats, pease, beans buckwheat, rye and corn and there is not one single word of complaint about foul seeds. Page 11 of this report deals with hay and clover and hay and clover seed, and there is not one single word of complaint from the correspondents of foul

If the complaints are general throughout Ontario, surely these correspondents who are practical farmers, would have drawn the attention of the provincial authorities to these serious complaints. We know that in Ontario it is at present an offence to allow thistles to grow on the highways and the farms, but that law is not observed. What is the use of enacting a stringent law of this kind, when we know it is impossible to carry it out. I do not believe that any farmer in this House could guarantee that the seed lie sells is actually pure, and if this law is passed you would prohibit a farmer from selling his seed if there is even a small percentage of foul seed in it. If this law cannot be carried out, it will do more harm than good. The best guarantee that you can hare against foul weeds, is to have first-

class farmers who will look after the cultivation of their crops.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: These answers read hv the hon. gentlemen are sent in to the provincial Department of Agriculture on special forms of questions which are prepared, and there is no question on that form with regard to weeds. They are statistics as to the crop and its general condition, and the questions include no reference to weeds, so that the hon. gentleman's criticism is not well founded. A good many of the provisions of this Bill only apply to clover and grass seeds, so that if my hon. friend would study the measure he would find it is not so drastic as he seems to think.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: My experience is that some legislation along the lines suggested by this Bill is very desireable. I know a good many farmers who have had their farms poisoned by foul weeds, and there is a general opinion amongst the farmers of my locality that some legislation of this kind should be adopted by parliament.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. minister, that in my locality a number of farmers have purchased turnip seed in which there was a good deal of foul rape seed and that has done a great deal of damage. I am sorry the minister does not provide against that in this Bill. It would not be well to have the provisions of this measure too drastic, but at the same time there certainly should be some legislation passed in this direction.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: The minister is mistaken when he says that these correspondents make no reference to weeds. Here is a report in regard to spring wheat in which it is said that the crop is good in point of yield and quality. They would not say that the quality of the grain is good if there were foul seed in it. Then again, in reference to the grass crop, it is stated in one of these reports that it is not of good quality, and if that were caused by reason of foul seeds, surely it would be so stated. I am not a practical farmer, but I do know that practical farmers are not in such a fortunate position to deal with this matter as are the managers of the government farms, backed up by any amount of money. It is for the ordinary farmers of Canada who are trying to live by the products of their farms that we are legislating here, and we should be careful not to pass any law which will militate against the interests of this most deserving class of the community.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: It appeal's to me that unless the merchant was able to have the seed which he sells tested,-which of course could not be done in most cases,-it would be impossible for him to know whether 90 per cent of the seed would germinate as is required in the Bill.

Mi-. RICHARDSON. The objects aimed at by this Bill are of the most desirable character. Nothing could he more important in the interests of the farming community than that the country should, if possible, be rid of the noxious weeds that infest it. But, to pass legislation of a character so onerous, so tyrannical, and with such heavy penalties as are provided in this Bill, is a very serious matter, when you may have it directed against persons who have no dishonest intention whatever.
We have had in the province of Ontario for a long time a law to prevent the spread of thistles, and to have them cleared away from the highways, but that law is inoperative. I do not think it should be. It is one that could be enforced much more easily than the Bill we have before us, which on its face is of an impracticable character. It is desirable that some regulation should be placed within the reach of every farmer which would enable him to have an inspection and analysis made of the seeds he buys, and to have it made free ; and the farmers should be invited as much as possible to have this inspection made. But after having made that provision, it is rather drastic legislation to provide that every one engaged in the seed business, and who may not have the skill or ability to analyse seeds, shall be liable to such heavy penalties as are provided in this Bill. These are of a character to render it inoperative and impractical. * While in full sympathy with the object aimed at, I think the Bill should be of such a practical character that it could be put into operation, and, while safeguarding the interests of the dealer and the producer, would also safeguard the interests of the farmer who buys seed for his own use.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I have had considerable experience, not only in growing seeds but in selling them. The law for the prevention and destruction of thistles growing on the highway is entirely different from the Bill now before this House. A farmer is not going to complain against his neighbour because he allows thistles to grow on his wayside, for he does not think it desirable to have the enmity of bis nearest neighbour. But I can assure you that if a farmer buys from a seed merchant a hundred pounds of clover, and finds after he has sown it that there is a lot of foul seed in it, he Will have no qualms of conscience about hauling the seed merchant over the coals and making him responsible for the damage done to his farm. I am delighted that something has been done by the Minister of Agriculture on this matter. We have been labouring too long in the province of Ontario under the evil of foul seeds, and it is time we had some redress, if any one has any doubt of this, let him take the Canada Atlantic and go from here to the town of Arnprior when the fields are ripening, and if he does not see the necessity of a Bill, of this kind, he

will certainly be very blind indeed. With reference to what the hon. member for Both-well (Mr. Clancy) says in regard to a stereotyped resolution being passed everywhere, 1 do not know7 whether that hon. gentleman has the power of being omnipresent or not; but I can assure him that the farmers of South Renfrew are intelligent enough to frame a resolution for themselves, and do not require a stereotyped resolution ; and I hurl the accusation back in the hon. gentleman's teeth with all the force of w7hich I am capable.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.

At every meeting this question of foul seeds was discussed, not only by these men, but by the farmers, and at every one of these meetings resolutions were passed extolling in the highest terms the action taken by the Minister of Agriculture on this subject. I know from the experience I have had in selling seeds that something of this kind should be done. Another thing to which my attention has been drawn, and which has not been brought out by the Minister of Agriculture, is that w7hen the farmers go to buy clover seed they cannot tell whether they are getting late or early clover ; and it w7ould be w7ell if the label which the Bill provides shall be attached to each package of seeds, giving the name of the kind of seeds, should state w7hether it is late or early clover. The Minister of Agriculture has received one testimonial w7hich is not among those he has read to-day. That testimonial came from the hon. member for Bothwell, w7ho tells us that he attended just one Farmers' Institute meeting, and that at that meeting he noticed that there w7as not a single individual opposed to this Bill. Mr. GIL'MOUR. I will say at once that I am in favour of this Bill or any ott)er Bill that would carry out the purpose intended. maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks me whether the seed merchants have protested or whether they have agreed to the

provisions of this Act. I would say in the first place that I have not understood that the seed merchants took exception to the general provisions of this Act. But they have protested against the provision to which my bon. friend has just alluded, and by which the farmers are allowed to sell to their neighbours and escape the provisions of the law; They have also pointed out certain difficulties in living up to the Act, but I do not think those "difficulties have a risen with regard to the quality of the seeds. I think that the seed merchants have practically accepted the provisions of sections 3 and 4 which indicate the grades. There is one point in this, however, in which the seed merchants differ from this Bill. They are quite ready to adopt what they called a minimum standard. below which no seed should be sold in the country at all. for grass and clover seeds. I understand they are willing to accept a minimum standard and object to any grading above that standard. This Act does not grade but it provides that if a merchant chooses to put a certain specimen of grain and mark it No. 1 quality or anything to indicate superior excellence, under those circumstances it must come up to a certain grade. And it indicates what that means in section 4 :
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have In his possession for sale, any seeds of timothy, red clover, alslke, or any mixture, containing the said seeds, in or from any receptacle, package, sack er. hag upon which is marked ' No. 1 ' or any other designation which represents such seeds as of first quality, unless they are free from the seeds of weeds named in section 3 of this Act.
Then it goes on :
And contain out of every 100 seeds not less than 99 seeds of the kind or kinds represented, or seeds of other useful and harmless grasses and clovers, of which 99 seeds 90 must he germmable.
That is the distinction we think necessary to justify the marketing of seed as No. 1 or of the highest quality. If seedsmen say that is too severe, they need not mark their seed. In the Act last year we undertook to fix the different grades. In this Act we do not. We fix a minimum grade below which no seed can be sold by anybody. That is, there must not be more than three seeds in the thousand that are seeds of certain weeds. The seed merchants who have discussed the matter with me seem to think that this is a grade that would be quite practicable.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I would like to ask why it is that when some clovers are included in this Bill, alfalfa is not included also ?

This Bill does not pretend to deal with the whole question. We would be very glad to go much further, if we felt we could do so successfully. We have un-Mr. FISHER.'
dertaken in this Bill to deal with the most common seeds that are sold. And I think I am safe in saying that, of the grass and clover seeds, that are sold in this country, the three kinds here named alike, red clover and timothy would cover, from 95 to 98 per cent of the sales. If we can get the country educated up to the point of dealing with these we can later on deal with those which are sold in less quantity.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Alfalfa is sold in my county to a large extent.

speechtext: Section 4 provides that 99 seeds out of 100 are to be of the kind or kinds represented. Then, of what kinds may the hundredth seed be ?

speechtext: It would not be permissible to have the hundredth seed that of any of the kinds mentioned in sections 3 and 4 ?

speechtext: No. As has been pointed out to me, a pound of red clover consists of 350,000 seeds. One in a hundred would be 3,500 seeds. That would be a very lai'ge proportion of noxious weed seeds and seed so foul could not be classed as No. 1.

speechtext: Have the seedsmen represented that it is possible to have grass seed without having more than one seed in one hundred that of one of these weeds ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: My question referred to germination.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
So far as that is concerned, it is easy for a man to test the germinating power of his seeds in a week or ten days. He might want to sell the seeds within a day or two of buying them it is true. I am advised that a man accustomed to handling seeds can judge pretty fairly by the look of the seeds as to its power of germination. But, in any case the seed laboratory is at

speechtext: If I understood the hon. minister, he said that he had sent out an officer of the department throughout Ontario to purchase samples of seeds in different places, and he told us some of the results. I understand the Minister of Agriculture to say that it does exist in the province of Ontario. As 1 understand it, suppose I raise seed not entirely pure and sell it to a seedsman, there would be no penalty on me. I think the Minister of Agriculture made too wide an assertion when he said that no foul seed could be sold under this Bill, because I think I can raise grass seed not entirely pure and sell it on my own premises, or sell it to a seedsman, and no penalty could be imposed on me under this Bill. Now, I want to ask the minister if any machinery has been invented whereby a seedsman can clean the seed and make it pure ? Suppose that I raised foul timothy seed and took it to a seedsman, is there any machinery whereby that merchant can clean it and bring it up to the standard ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I am informed that there is undoubtedly machinery which will bring it up to the minimum standard. As to bringing it up to the maximum standard, it would depend a little on the nature of the impurities in the seed. But a great deal of even pretty foul seed can be brought up to the first quality mentioned under this Act by machinery which is well known, and which Is in use to-day among the seedsmen of the country. I may say to my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) that I have such a list as 1 mentioned from every one of the provinces

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I listened to what the minister said with regard to the situation of the seedsmen under this Bill, and I must admit that my experience is not like hi3, because wherever I have conversed with seedsmen with regard to the Bill of last year, they said they could not comply with its provision, that if such a law was enacted it would compel them to go out of the business. I admit the desirability of a law that will give us pure seed, but I do not think the present Bill will accomplish that end. The only question to my mind is whether, if this Act is passed, it can be made workable. It seems to me there are a few provisions that go too far. For instance, section 3 says :
No person shall sell, or offer, expose, or have in his possession for sale, for the purpose of seeding, any seeds of cereals, grasses, clovers or forage plants containing any seeds of the following weeds.

Then follows a list of the weed seeds. The section goes on :
Unless each and every receptacle, package, sack or bag containing such seeds, or a label, securely attached thereto, ;s marked in a plain and indelible manner-
(a.) with the initials of the Christian names, and the full surname and address of the wholesale or retail seller ;
(b ) with the name of the kind or kinds of
see i .	*
(c.l with the common name or names of the aforenamed weeds, the seeds of which are present in the seed sold or offered, exposed or had in possession for sale.
Now if I correctly understand that seetiou, every package containing the seed for sale must have the initial of the wholesaler or retailer upon it, as well as the kind of seed Contained in it, with the names of the weed seeds present, and a list of those is given Now take oats for instance. The seedsman usually keeps his oats in a bin. You want to purchase some seed oats and he takes them out of that hin. As I understand this section, he would require to have upon that bin the name of all the weed seeds present in those oats.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Only those that are mentioned here.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
Wild oats is among the names of weed seeds mentioned here. The name ' wild oats ' has to be put on every bin containing oats, because there are few lots of oats which do not contain wild oats. Then we find mentioned bindweed, per-rennial sow-thistle, ragweed, great ragweed, purple coc-kle, cow cockle, orange hawkweed or paint brush, ergot of rye, and some others. Every one of these weeds, if the cereal contains any of these seed weeds, must be marked on the bin containing the oats, or on the bag, or whatever receptacle they are sold in. I think this provision will pretty surely be ignored. I do not think one seedsman out of a hundred would attempt to carry that out, and a law that cannot be carried out is worse than useless, because not only does it do no good, but it creates a contempt for law. Then section 4 says :
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, any seeds of timothy, red clover, alsike or any mixture containing the said seeds, in or from any receptacle, package, sack or bag upon which is marked ' No. 1 ' or any other designation which represents such seeds as of first quality, unless they are free from the seeds of weeds named in section 3 of this Act.
If he sells the seed as No. 1, it means he sells it as of the first quality, and it can only contain a certain percentage of weed seeds. Then the seed must also contain a certain percentage that will germinate. Now, how is the purchaser to tell whether every seed will germinate or not ? Suppose a quantity Mr. SPROULE.
of seed sold as being of the first quality was found to contain more weed seeds in the crop than is allowed, or a greater percentage of seeds that did not grow than is allowed under this Bill, and an action for damages was instituted against the seedsman, how are you to prove it ?
There has been no sample taken in advance to enable you to ascertain what percentage of seeds is germinable and what is not, and to ascertain what percentage of weed seeds is contained in it. I take it that if seeds are sold under this Act as No. 1, or first quality, it will leave the seedsmen open to an action at law if it is found afterwards that the seeds which he sold injures a man's farm or .if they contain weeds when they were supposed to contain no *weeds. But, an action cannot be maintained under this Act because of tbe difficulty of proving the offence to the court. It seems to me that this makes the law in that respect unworkable, and I think in some other respects as well it is unworkable. While it appears to be an improvement on the Bill that was introduced last year, I think still that it would be utterly impossible for seedsmen to comply with its provisions. The hon. Minister of Agriculture said that it is an easy matter to use machinery to clean the seed so that it will come up to the minimum standard, not the'maximum standard. My experience and information are that weed seeds are taken out by sieves and where you have weed seeds of about the same size as the ordinary grass 'or clover seed you are cleaning, it is absolutely impossible for any machinery in the world to do that work, and to make the grass seed perfectly clean.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
I presume the discussion regarding the quality of seeds in the province of Ontario must have arisen because Ontario province is the great producer of seeds in Canada. Perhaps you might say that the entire crop of red clover and alsike not of timothy, though a large proportion of timothy may be included-is produced in Ontario, and this is due to the fact that the other provinces either do not grow these seeds or their climatic conditions are found unsuitable. I was very much impressed with the general provisions of the Bill introduced last year. I think there is no observant member of this House or observant Canadian who travels through this country, especially at this season of the year and now on for the next two or three weeks, but will notice that the crops of hay and often times grain as well are sadly spoiled by the large proportion of weeds which are growing in them. To whom that is due we cannot tell. Whether it is due to the carelessness of the man on the farm or the man who sells him the seed, the fact is that the weeds seem to have spread over the entire country. The wild mustard seems to be increasing at an alarming rate. Although

certain scientists have discovered that by spraying it can be killed, that process, I have been informed, has not been found altogether satisfactory. This is one of the most noxious weeds we have. However, the fact is that the country is being fast overrun with weeds. Under these circumstances if this House could bring forth a proper measure which would regulate the evil in such a way as to prevent the spread of weed seeds, it would be a boon to the country. But it seems to me that a great deal must depend upon the man who cultivates the farm. If he will continue to sow seed that is bad he must of course have all the weeds which go with it, and the consequences. I am not opposing this Bill at all, but I want to criticise it and I want to hear from other members of the House in regard to it. I feel that the difficulty is in the actual working of the Act. I have been accustomed to handling seeds nearly all my life and the great difficulty I see is in connection with the working of the Act. I am a little afraid that in this Bill we have something in the nature of paternal legislation, that we are undertaking to look after the business of the man who should look after his own interests. I. have sometimes thought, as I have listened to the discussions upon different Bills in this House, that we have too much paternal legislation. I do not presume to call this Bill paternal legislation, and I feel with the majority in this House that something should be done whether this Bill is in the right direction or not. We had a Bill last year and I thought some of its provisions very drastic indeed. After we had discussed it and after I had thought over it during the recess, I felt that the Bill should be modified in some way. It has been modified in the Bill, which is now before the committee, but, looking at the clauses, there are some features of it yet which would need some modification. Take clause 4, for instance : it seems to me that when you say that of every 100 seeds, not less than 99 shall be of the kind or kinds represented it is rather high. In red clover there are some hard seeds and it would be very difficult to comply with that clause. If it were put at 97 or 98 seeds the proportion would be a little better. Then, it states that of those 99 seeds, 90 must be germinable. Ninety per cent is a high standard of germination. Almost any one who is accustomed to dealing -with seeds day after day, and having perhaps a dozen or two dozen samples presented to him can tell what proportion will grow. A real expert seed buyer will be able to tell yon a week after a crop has been offered to him by sample, just what proportion of the crop will grow. I think if the number of germinable seeds was made 85 instead of 90, it would be a better proportion. Then, the minimum clause is an improvement upon the provision of last year's Bill. The minimum clause provides that:
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, for the purpose of seeding in Canada, any seeds of timothy, al-sike or red clover, or any mixture containing the said seeds, if the seeds of the weeds named in sections 3 and 4 of this Act are present in a greater proportion than three to one thousand of the seed sold, or offered, exposed or held in possession for sale.
In case there were a million and a quarter seeds in timothy, that would give 3,750 seeds which would be allowed which is a fair proportion, and if there were 3,750 seeds of that kind allowed in a pound, I should think that would be sufficient. In regard to clause 8 the penalty is very serious for such an offence. It provides that any one who violates the provisions of the Act shall for each offence, be liable to a fine for the first offence not exceeding $5 and not less than $1. Suppose you load a cai with 200 bags of seed, and suppose that all the hags were found not to comply with the provisions of the Act, if you had 200 bags which do not comply with the provisions of the Act, and you had to pay $5 each in fines that would amount to $1,000 on a carload of seed. I think, that, considering, the value of a car of seed, it is an enormous fine to impose. This Bill is designed to regulate a very old and valuable trade, a trade which is very largely carried on in the interest of the country. The capital invested in the province of Ontario in farming operations is over a billion dollars and that is all at stake in connection with every farm that there is in this great province, because every farmer sows seed. Under these circumstances, I think that the fine should be as small as it is possible, considering the interests which are at stake, and that it should not be any higher than is necessary to regulate this old standard trade. Recognizing the rapid spread of weeds throughout the country, I think that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) is to be commended for the steps he has taken to check this evil. The establishment of a seed laboratory and the distribution throughout the country of information regarding noxious weed seeds, their habits and how to kill them and regarding the germination .of seeds haw' given the farmers an immense advantage. If the majority of the House think, that this Bill will regulate the seed trade, I am prepared to support it. I am prepared to support the minister in anything that is right and proper in connection with this matter. I believe that in a year or two after this plan of education has gone on a little further, possibly we may be able to get a Bill which will suit every interest. I am not saying that the present Bill does not suit every interest now, but looking at it from the ordinary experience of every day business life, I can see that even this Bill, which is aii improvement on last year's Bill, may require to he amended from

time to time in accordance with existing conditions.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I appreciate the support which my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Ross) has given to this Bill, and I may say that most of the difficulties which he has pointed out are of minor detail which can be very easily modified. As to the fines, it can be very easily arranged that where only one package is sold the penalty shall be so much per package, but if there be a large number of packages sold, the aggregate penalty should not exceed a certain reasonable amount. I shall be glad to consider that in committee.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Did the correspondence which the minister has had in connection with this Bill between last session and this, include any correspondence from the representatives of the different provinces. Has he had the co-operation of the provincial ministers of agriculture ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I am reminded now, that there is a letter from the Deputy Minister of Agriculture of British Columbia, and also a letter, or perhaps more than one, from the Hon. Mr. Elliot, Commissioner of Agriculture in the Northwest Territories. 1 think there are one or two letters from Mr. Ferris, of New Brunswick, and possibly from Mr. Dryden, of Ontario, but I am not sure.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: One would have thought that the minister would have communicated with these gentlemen who represent the agricultural departments of the different provinces. Has the minister sent a copy of this Bill to the ministers of agriculture for each province ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I do not know if it was sent to the ministers, but it was sent to the deputy head of the department in each province, so that it was thoroughly understood and known in the departmental offices.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Just in a formal way ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext:
The same as it was sent everywhere else. In reply to my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Ross), I would say that the provisions of this Bill are about as mild as they can be to accomplish the object in view. I am much gratified to find throughout the counlty a very great awakening on this subject, and I have most gratifying testimony from the farmers as *well as from the seed merchants of the good results from the investigation by my department, and from the discussions that have arisen. There is no doubt that in the last tnree years there has been a very considerable improvement in the handling ot seeds throughout Canada, and a very general demand on the part of the farmers for better seeds, which has lea to an improvement in the seeds offered for sale. There
is to-day a considerable quantity of refuse seed some of which is sold in this country and this Bill aims to do away with that absolutely. My hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) asked me about the methods of cleaning seeds. As a farmer I never myself raised seed, having always bought it.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Have you done any ploughing ?

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Quite a lot. I have never raised a crop of seed for sale, but I am informed by those who have, that the seed merchants who have complete machinery for the cleaning of seed, can clean it so as to live up 'to the provisions of this Act. The system of screens and sieves is only a part of the best cleaning machinery ; there is a system of drafts and blowers-

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: That is done by the fanning mill.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Yes, but the results do not depend upon the size of the seed. The ungerminable seeds are much lighter as a rule and they are blown away ; even an ordinary fanning mill properly worked can almost always clean the dirtiest grass seed.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: Not the ordinary fanning mill.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: The Chatham mill can.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I believe the Chatham mill is a very good one, and is quite capable of cleaning the dirtiest seed. But any good fanning mill can clean seed so as to bring it up to the minimum standard fixed in the Bill, as a general rule. Therefore, I feel that with proper care, with care that we may fairly ask should be exercised by a person engaged in this trade, the seed merchants can live up to the conditions of this Bill. When the seedsmen interviewed me a little while ago, I think I am correct in saying that their chief objection was to that clause of the Bill which allows farmers to sell seed to their neighbours without being subject to the conditions of the Bill. I have kept that clause in the Bill, because I have felt that a farmer buying from his neighbour has not only the protection of requiring the seller, if he choses, to sell to him subject to the provisions of this Act and to give him a certificate, but he has also the protection of knowing from his own observation whether his neighbour's field from which he has taken the seed was clear and clean or not. He has this special protection which the ordinary purchaser has not. The farmer is not allowed under this Act to sell promiscuously. He is only allowed to sell to his neighbour on his own premises.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: He is allowed to sell to the merchant as well.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: He is allowed to sell to the merchant seeds to be cleaned. He can

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: only sell on his premises seeds to be used for seed purposes. Otherwise, under section 7 he can only sell seeds for the purpose of food, or to merchants to be cleaned or graded before being offered for sale. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that he would forbid a farmer selling seeds to a seed merchant? If he did, he would stop the whole trade in the country.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: No, I do not. But 1 ask the hon. minister whether it would not be better to fix a minimum standard, and leave it at that, instead of making provisions for three or four different grades which no person can comply with. I would be very suspicious of a seed merchant who would make these marks. I would rather take the mark of a firm of standing that had been in existence for forty or fifty years, such as that of which my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Bruce) is at the head.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to have lost sight of the fact that this Bill simply requires the minimum standard, but that if a seedsman wishes to label his seed as of No. 1 quality, he has to comply with certain provisions. Would my hon. friend think it wise not only to fix a minimum standard, but to allow every seedsman to call that No. 1 quality ? I do not think the farmers of this country are prepared to say that that should be done. '

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: The word of the man who has been in business for thirty or forty years that the seed is pure would be sufficient.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: There are people engaged in the seed business whose word is as good as the bond of other people ; but there are a lot of other people engaged, in it not of the same standing, and there are others who are selling seed at second and third hand, and we should apply machinery to prevent these people doing what they ought not to do. Nobody need do more than live up to the minimum standard, but if any one undertakes to tell a farmer that a seed is of first quality, he is required to comply with the condition of section 4. With regard to section 3, it is an actual concession. It provides that a man may sell seeds with those weeds in them, provided he says what weeds are in them. It is not a dominating clause ; it is a concession to the seedsmen of the country.

maintopic: THE INSPECTION AND SALE OF SEEDS.
speechtext: I have not consulted any seedsmen in regard to this measure ; but if I were a seedsman and had to comply with the provisions of this Bill, I would just label my seeds according to the minimum standard, and would then tell the purchasers which was pure seed.
