I notice that, in this item, there is an increase of .$10,000 over the expenditure of last year. What is the explanation of this 7

I may say, in the first place, that i am asking additional sums in the supplementary estimates for the current year, which will soon be brought down. A very considerable proportion of this increase is due to the increase in wages and salaries on the farms, which has been found absolutely necessary. We have the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa and four branch farms, and they employ in the aggregate-I am making rather a guess-between eighty and ninety men, in addition to the staff of officers. Wages have gone up generally throughout the country. I was informed a little while ago that if I did not immediately increase the wages on the farms at In-'dian Head and Brandon, all the men on them would leave. These were experienced men who had been a good while on the farms, and we found, as a matter of fact, that we were not paying wages equal to the farm wages of the community around. I wao obliged, therefore, to agree to an increase of from 20 to 25 per cent all round on the ordinary wages of these farms.
What is the rate of wages on these farms 7

The foremen are the highest paid men, then the teamsters, then the men in the barns attending the cattle, and then the labourers. I find that on the Experimental Farm at Ottawa one teamster is entered here on the list at $8.75 per week for last year.
And has to board himself ?
Yes. This case may be taken as a criterion of the wages. You could not keep the man at the wages paid.
What do the labourers get 7
About $7' or $7.50 a week.
And have to board themselves ?
Yes. We do not board men on any of the farms. On each of the western farms there is a boarding house, but the men have to pay their board at these houses.
How many hours do they work 7

The teamsters and labourers work ten hours. The men who take charge of the cattle and work inside the barns begin a little earlier and stop a little later, but their work is supposed to be lighter and nicer work, and they get paid for Sundays, because they have to be there on Sundays. Besides the ordinary wages, we had to increase the pay all along the line, including the pay of the officials. I am Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
proud to say that in the Director of Experimental Farms, Professor Saunders, and the other officials, we have a very efficient staff of experienced experts, men who have shown by their work there how valuable they are to the country, and how thoroughly equipped for their duties. There is a very considerable demand, not only in Canada, but in the United States, for expert service, and we have to pay these men proportionately to what similar men get elsewhere for similar work. And I have even had to contend with direct offers from other countries to these gentlemen to tempt them away. As a Canadian 1 am proud of the fact that these men, who are also Canadians, are so well treated and so satisfied to remain in the service of Canada, that some of them at any rate have refused offers of considerably higher pay in oilier places: rajther than leave their work here. They are devoted and enthusiastic to their work on the Experimental Farm, they take an interest in their work, a pride in it, and several of them have refused to leave it for higher pay and go elsewhere. These offers come from a foreign country. In view of this fact, and with my knowledge of these men, their energy and capacity, and in view of the fact that in other walks of life all through the country men are being paid higher than they were two years ago, I hare felt bound in the interests of the experimental farms as well as in the interest of these gentlemen, to increase their salaries. These increases have been going on for the last year or two, and the result is that the item which was voted last year of $90,000 will not be sufficient to jiay the expenses of the farm for the current year. I shall therefore be obliged to ask for $10,000 more for this year's work. I had a conversation on this matter with Prof. Saunders, and we agreed that we could not carry out the work required on the farm without more money.
Are the labourers employed throughout the year ?

Most of them are. We have to dispense with a few of them in the autumn, but during the winter we employ as many of them as we can on what is called the seed distribution. During the winter we put up tens of thousands packages of, seeds, which are sent out over the country to the farmers, and in this work we employ men who are not engaged in the Held and in the barns. There are generally a few men on each of these farms who are not employed all the time during the winter, but practically a good employee is given work nearly the -whole year round. I am informed that the increase of wages and salaries would not be less than 25 per cent on tne old rate. I am also informed that we have increased the staff somewhat, and witu the increase of the staff, the increase

of wages and the increase of salaries, we will use up $75,000 out of this $100,000.
How much is the labourer getting ?
The common labourer is getting the same as the city labourer, $1.50 for a working day. Teamsters get a little more, and foremen a little more still.
What increases, if any, have been made in the staff at the Nappan farm, and what are the wages paid to the men employed there ?

Tnere is no increase in tlie staff at Nappan. There is a slight increase in the number of labourers there. The pay of the labourers is about on the same scale as the pay at the central farm. But on the western farms in Brandon, Iuuian Head and British Columbia, the pay is higher. We cannot get labour there at the same price.
Mr. LOGaj. What is the pay of the labouring man at Nappan ?
Ordinary labour runs from $1.40 to $1.60 a day, the men boarding themselves. Of course there are some skilled labourers who get higher wages than that.
How many employees are there on the central and other experimental farms ?

On the Central Experimental Farm, excluding the officers, there are about fifty employees. There are ten or twelve men, varying a little as the seasons go, on the branch farms making a total altogether of very nearly one hundred employees.
In addition to them how many skilled labourers have you ?
That includes the skilled labourers-all except the officers.
How many officers have you ?

Nine. At the Central Experimental Farm there is the director, Prof. Saunders, Prof. Fletcher the botanist and entymologist. Prof. Shutt. chemist. Prof. Grisdale. agriculturist and Prof. Macoun, horticulturist, making five officers proper. Then besides that there is Mr. Gilbert in charge of the poultry, Mr. Fortier his assistant and in the office they have three stenographers, an accountant and assistant clerk. Mr. Fletcher has two assistants in his work. Mr. Shutt has two assistants in the laboratory and there are two clerks in the office. That I think covers the whole staff. That makes altogether at the Central Experimental Farm, including officers, office staff and assistants, foremen and employees in the neighbourhood of seventy-five. * On each branch farm there is a farm manager
and a book-keeper or secretary to the manager who has to do stenographic work and keep the books. On the farm at Nappan there is a horticulturist. The other farms have no such officers. Mr. Sharp, in British Columbia, is himself a horticulturist and there is no fruit growing to speak of at Indian Head or Brandon.
Have you not a horticulturist and a bee-keeper at the Central Farm ?
Prof. Macoun who is the horticulturist of the whole system is here and he has under him an orchard foreman and a garden foreman. The farm foreman, Mr. Fixter, takes care of the bees.

Would the hon minister give us a statement of the wages paid to the labourers on the different farms so that we will have an opportunity of knowing what the current rate of wages in the different parts of Canada is ?
Mr. FISHER, The rate of pay here for the common labourer is $1.50 a day, that is the usual rate of labour in the city. At Nappan it is about the same. There may be one or two men who only get $1.40 a day although I do not believe that there are. At the three western farms the pay is $1.75 a day.
Does that include board and lodging ?
They pay for their own board and lodging at all of the farms.
When the hon. gentleman took office what did these labouring men get ?
I am informed that the ordinary labourer was paid at that time $1 a day in the winter and $1.25 a day in summer at Ottawa. I have no details of what was paid in the west.

What difference do you make now between wages in winter and summer, if any ?
Mr. FISHER, Now, they generally average a dollar less per week in winter than in summer.
The hon. minister mentioned some increases in salaries and some additions to the staff of officers that he proposes to make. Will he give us a statement of these ?

I think perhaps I did not express myself correctly. I have been increasing the staff and salaries. The actual scale on the farms to-day requires this extra $10,000 to meet the increases which have been made in salaries and-in the staff. During the last year I have appointed Dr. Charles E. Saunders to the office of experimentalist here. That has reference to plant breeding. Dr. Saunders the director has himself for many years been conducting ex-

periments in the breeding of plants, the breeding of new varieties both of wheat and fruit. This is a very special class of work requiring expert knowledge and treatment. I found very soon that Prof. Saunders was overburdened with the work and responsibility that were thrown upon him, and that it was impossible for him to continue to deal with this work which requires extraordinary attention to detail. At certain seasons of the year the experimentalist has to watch very closely every little detail and every change in connection with the experiment which he is carrying on. It was utterly impossible for the director to do this and attend to the general management of the whole of the farms. I felt it necessary to have somebody who would be specially charged with this work. There was some assistance which a new man coming in would be able to render the director and relieve him of some of the very onerous duties which he had been carrying on for many years and in the performance of which he practically endangered his health. Dr. Charles Saunders is an expert in this particular work. There are very few in Canada who have studied and practised plant and fruit breeding and I was glad to secure the services of a gentleman who had studied under Dr. Saunders, and who had shown expert knowledge. Within the last year I was obliged to appoint another assistant chemist to cope with the increased work. Mr: H. W. Charlton was appointed to this office, I think two years ago, but it is an increase the full effects of which we are trying to meet this year by the supplementary vote.
It is not an increase, if be was here last year.

It is not an increase for next year, but I will be obliged to ask for a supplementary vote of $10,000 so as to overtake arrears. I do not expect any increase next fiscal year. The work that is done on the farm to-day would require for this fiscal year $100,000, and I am asking $100,000 for next year. We had to pay during the currrent year certain amounts, the obligations for which were incurred last fiscal year, when I did not get any extra vote.
What are the arrears ?

It is rather hard to say which individual thing incurred these arrears. There were a number of expenditures incurred last year which the vote of last year did not meet and which had to be paid out of the vote of this year. I believe that the supplementary vote of $10,000 will clear up all the expenses to the end of this fiscal year, and I hope $100,000 will be sufficient to cover entirely the expenditure of the next fiscal year. I also added Mr. Fortier as an assistant to Mr. Gilbert in the poultry division. Mr. Gilbert's time Mr. FISHER.
has been so taken up with addressing public meetings and institutes and forwarding information with inference to poultry, that he has not been able to undertake any new experimental work for several years back, and for which there is a great necessity. There have been greatly increased demands from the French Canadian farmers of the province of Quebec for information about everything connected with poultry, and I felt it would be very important to have a gentleman who could give explanations in French as Mr. Gilbert does in English. Mr. Fortier commences with $700 per year ; he was engaged last September or October.
Is he provided with a house ?
No. $700 is all he gets and of course his travelling expenses. Last autumn there was an additional typewriter put into the office whose name is I think, Mr. Dupuis, or something like that.
Does that include all in connection with what you call salaried officials ?

I am just informed that last year there was a Miss Hagar added to the staff at $480 a year. This young lady was employed at some special tabulated work of a scientific character in connection with the results of some experiments.
How many employees were on this farm in 1896 7
I could not say off-hand.
How many were there three years ago ?

I can only give an estimate which has been made on the spur of the moment by the director, that there are about four now where there were three then. There are about 100 on all the farms, of whom about 75 are on the central farm. The officers and office staff number about 25 and the farm employees about 50.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us the cost of the salaried officials of the Central Experimental Farm ?

The total amount of the salaries for all the farms, including the .managers of the branch farms and the office help, is $33,498. The Auditor General's Report shows that the salaried officials of the central farm last year cost $23,296. It would be a little more now, owing to the increases which I have mentioned. The wages paid to all employees below the salaried officials amount to the following : Central, $21,000 ; Nappan, $4,800 ; Brandon, $5,600 ; Indian Head, $5,300 ; Agassiz, $4,400.

I notice by the report of the minister on the experimental farms that

some experiments were made at Nappan in the keeping of bees, and the only report on them that I can find is the following :
Six colonies were put into winter quarters last December. All died during the winter.
This does not give us very much information on bee-keeping. The report should give us the reason why all these died. The weather is no colder down there than in other parts of Canada where bees are successfully kept.

I have not any further information on that point, except that the director informs me that all over Canada last winter there was an extraordinary mortality of bees. If there had been any special reason for the death of the bees in that case, 1 think it would have been stated in the report.
It seems rather remarkable that they all died, that there was not a single bee left. I think bees flourished in other parts of the country.

It is a strange thing that we are paying gentlemen of scientific knowledge to keep bees, and the only information we have is that they all died. We have not a bee left to tell the story. AVe have a Minister of Agriculture, and when we ask him for information he cannot give it. What is he here for ? I want to tell the hon. gentleman that there are plenty of men keeping bees in the riding which I represent, and those bees did not all die. AVe have an experimental farm, and I, as a farmer, am prepared to pay any reasonable amount for the management of the experimental plots ; but I am not prepared to pay for a deputy to take care of hens, and when we ask for information the minister tells us he has not all the details. The details of the hen department are something like those of the bee department-we have an account of what we pay, but not of what we receive from it. I am willing that we should pay any reasonable amount for thi experimental plots, but when it comes to paying nearly $22,000 for help on a farm of some 200 or 300 acres, it is difficult not to enter a protest. In my opinion, if the hon. minister cannot make the farm pay, leaving the experimental plots out of the question, he should get out of the business. How many acres in that farm ?
465, of which 200 are worked as a stock farm, and with the exception of the ground taken lip by the buildings and their surroundings the rest is devoted to experimental work.
And we pay $21,000 for labour on that 200 acres ?

$21,000 covers all the labour, including experimental work, arboretum, vines and shrubberies, orchards, gardens and everything else.
.158

I have heard a good deal of that orchard. In our section of the country, we would not consider that orchard kept in proper condition at all. The farm, outside the experimental plots, should pay its way, especially a farm which has the advantage of the care of so many scientific men, and for which you can obtain any quantity of cheap manure in the city. If you cannot make it pay, what is the use of keeping it ? I see that we pay in the neighbourhood of $2,000 for feeding stock. AVhat experiment is there about feeding stock ? The farmers in the section I have the honour to represent know as much about feeding stock as any of the gentlemen on this farm. Unless the hon. gentleman can succeed by experiment in devising some method of feeding stock; cheaper than it costs now, there is no advantage in having stock on the farm at all. Judging by the information given us by the Agricultural Committee, if it costs as much to feed and fatten stock in our section as it does on the experimental farm, every farmer who feeds stock would lose money. AVhat is the use of experimenting in keeping milch cows if you cannot raise enough on that farm to feed them ? And all these men who are employed on the farm are kept around the buildings all winter. How long could the hon. minister run a farm of his own if he had to keep all the men employed all winter ?

The great bulk of the labour on the farm is expended on experimental work. In the farm report there is a full statement of the expenditure in connection with the 200 acre farm which is run as a stock farm. Out of 465 acres, only 200 are run that way. The rest are given to experimental work which brings in no return at all. But we have beeu complimented on that work over and over again by all sorts and conditions of people and from all sides of politics. The labour expended on that is much greater than the labour employed on the 200 acre farm which is set aside for stock. Over two-thirds of the whole wages are spent In experimental work and the work about the grounds and the arboretum and that kind of thing. There is an account kept at the farm of the labour on each branch, and although it would be a considerable task to work it up, I could obtain from the book-keeper a statement showing how much labour is charged against each individual piece of work. Page D-37 of the Auditor General's Report, contains a summary of this kind of work. At the bottom of the page the hon. gentleman will find a division on a certain scale of the different expenditures. This is not all wages.
Salaries of officials cover $23,296.29.

That is not wages at all. Just below that are the farm wages $21,000.



But if the hon. gentleman will look at the bottom of the page he will see a division of this expenditure under different headings. The different departments have some expenses besides labour.
I would like the hon. gentleman to explain the difference between ' farm work ' and ' care of stock. '

The hon. gentleman can put them together if he chooses. Farm work is one thing, but care of cattle includes a good deai of experimental work. When a man feeds cattle for experimental purposes, he must take a great deal more time than where cattle are fed merely with a view to profit. In the experimental work the feeding requires careful measuring, weighing and accounting, and all this means labour and expense.

If my information is correct, the hon. gentleman's experiment in fattening stock resulted in greater expense than we get for the beef in the section I represent. If that is the case, the experiment is useless.

I do not know what report the hon. gentleman refers to, but, as a rule the experiments in feeding at the farm have been profitable-that is they show that the farmer who carried on feeding in that way would make a profit.
Yes, that is very well, being in a city like Ottawa. But if that were carried on in my section, it might not pay.
Of course, we cannot work the farm at Ottawa as if it were in Northumberland.

But if its experiments are such that farmers in the country cannot carry them out, they are in reality a failure. He may make a success of feeding when he sells the beef at 75 cents to $1 pet-hundred more than we can get. But if we fed on that basis, we would be losing money.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) forgets another thing-that when the experiments are being carried on, different systems of feeding are tried one against the other. While all may show a profit, one will show more profit than others. Even where loss occurs, the information so gained is valuable to the farmer, because he needs to be warned against mistakes as well as advised what he should do. It is of the very nature of experiment that some things should fail.

How long does it take a scientific gentleman to arrive at a conclusion. The Minister of Agriculture, with his scientists about him has been experimenting for seven or eight /ears. How long a time is required ?

That depends on how much knowledge is required. If a man is Mr. FISHER.
contented with a little he can arrive at it very soon, but if he desires a great deal of knowledge it will take much more time to acquire it.

That is about as much satisfaction as we generally get. The minister takes a long time to explain, and when he reaches his conclusion, we are in just as satisfactory a position as we were before he commenced. Does he tell me and the farmers pf this country that it requires eight or nine years to come to the conclusion what is the best way of feeding an animal so that he may give us practical advice as to the way in which beef can be most cheaply produced ? .1 think it is worse than a humbug to talk to the farmers in that way, to tell us that it will take us long to get the information we want as the information we want is great. I am here to say that, at the end of eight or nine years scientific men should have been able to reach a conclusion as to the cheapest way to feed an animal.
I understand the scientific feeders of stock at the farm do not feed the same as my hon. friend from East Northumberland does.
I do not know how that hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) feeds.
I feed to make a little money.
If the hon. gentleman makes money, I congratulate him.

I understand the hon. minister to say that in the experimental feeding of stock different quantities are fed to different animals in the same group, whereas in the ordinary commercial feeding all would be fed the same. Of what advantage is this scientific feeding to the practical farmer ?	*

I was speaking of the difference in cost of the different methods of feeding. Even under ordinary conditions, a man, who is what we call a good feeder will recognize the difference of individuality in the animals, and he will give each the quantity of feed of which it can make the best use. We try experiments not with one animal, but with a group of animals.
The same herd.

The same herd. But we attempt to get groups of animals' which will as much as possible correspond with one another. Take, say, a dozen steers here and another dozen as nearly as possible like them in another group. We feed one group in one way all winter, or a certain number of months, and another group in another way for the same number of months, and note what the results are. I think the farmers will recognize that there is a good deal of individuality in each animal, and if we were to experiment with a single animal

the result would be of little value. We have to take large groups of animals in order to make a fait test. Sometimes we have even to duplicate the experiment before we are in a position to give forth 'a statement which the farmers may depend upon. In that respect I wish to compliment Prof. Saunders because he has been exceptionally careful, in sending out reports, to send only those upon which the farmers may rely and may base their work. I think the reputation of the experimental farms on this continent and wherever their reports reach, has been largely due to the fact that the work has been done with great care, and no hasty conclusions have been jumped at. If to-day the reports of the experimental farms are received as authoritative, it is due to the extreme care and accuracy with which experiments have been conducted. 1 do not think my hon. friend realizes the amount of extra work, of extra labour, of extra time and extra money which must be put upon these experiments to give them that character.

The hon. gentleman says he arrives at an average by experimenting with different groups of animals. We had one of the employees before the Agricultural Committee who told us that they fed one animal in one way, and another animal of the same herd and in the same stable in another way ; they were not grouped together in the way the minister describes.

There are different classes of experiments. The experiment he alluded to was feeding dairy cows, not herds. If the feeder was feeding a group of shorthorns he fed each individual in that group to the best advantage in order to show what that group could do, each of them was dealt with to the best advantage. Another group of cows was also dealt with, each to the best advantage. The experiment I referred to was where a group, say, of ten or a dozen steers were taken and fed in a certain way to see how much gain they would make in a certain period ; and another group were fed in a little different way. For instance, we have been making experiments between one group of steers loose and another group of steers tied up. but feeding them in exactly the same way in order to see which group would make the most gain. It is evident that it would be more economical for the ordinary farmer to feed his steers loose than to feed them tied up. if they made equally as much gain. We have had varying results. The first year the result of that experiment was a little different from the result of the second years experiment. Although we have now been going on for three years, we may have to go on three years more before we can arrive at such a conclusion as can be relied upon. Those that are tied are tied 1584
with a chain around the neck, and the chain is attached to an iron rod. I think the first seasons' work was in favour of the group that was tied up, and the next seasons' work was in favour of those that were loose. It is of great benefit to the farmers to be able to get such experiments made for them. In issuing these bulletins of the reports, we try to give as many details as we can without encumbering the statements.

The minister has spoken of experiments in feeding different herds of cattle, but these experiments must necessarily be made upon a large scale with a considerable number of animals. Does he think that the whole experiment is of general benefit to the ordinary farmer in the community ?

Yes. The ordinary farmdr does not need to do all these things for himself. After he has obtained the results from the experimental farm he can say : Such and such a method of feeding animals has been tried and proved to be the best. I will adopt that method.
Can he in reality practically follow the method prescribed in the bulletins ?
Yes, there is nothing, to hinder any farmer who keeps stock from feeding his animals in the same way as they are treated in the experimental farm.
Will the hon. minister say it is practicable for every farmer in the country to pursue the methods prescribed in these bulletins to his own pecuniary profit ?

Yes, there is no doubt whatever that if he would take the reports and bulletins as issued and use a little common sense in applying what he finds there to his own conditions and circumstances, he would be immensely benefited. As a matter of fact we know that a very large number of farmers do find that they are benefited because we get countless letters from farmers, some of them asking questions, but explaining that they have been very much interested in what they have read, that they have applied the methods and that they have derived great benefit from them.	[DOT]

If the farmers have been so much benefited by the information received from your bulletins why are you, going on with the experiments still ? The question is how long you are going to continue these experiments to arrive at a conclusion.

We will have to continue these experiments as long as the world goes on and agriculture lasts. There are constantly arising new problems to be dealt with in this country and to stop

where we are would simply be stopping after we had progressed only a small distance upon the road to the attainment of knowledge.
That is hifalutin.
It is not hifalutin. It is a simple fact and I am glad to know that we realize that in the agriculture of this continent there are problems which have to be solved.
We know all that.
Then the hon. gentleman knows it all.
No.

If the hon. gentleman does he is in a hopeless condition.
Mr. (JoCHRANB. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that I made no such statement. It is just such gentlemen as he that are in that deplorable condition that they know it all. There was a member of this House, Mr. McMillan, who satisfied himself years ago in reference to the feeding of animals tied up or loose in the stalls and that gentleman was one of the most practical men I ever met with here.
He was.
And he settled the question that the hon. gentleman is trying to experiment with.

Some hon. gentleman seemed to think it remarkable that I should ask the hon. minister how cattle should be tied. Of course they are not practical farmers and they do not understand it. Do I understand the hon. minister to approve any particular method of tying cattle in the stables ? Take milch cows.
If the hon. gentleman asks me as a farmer what I would do, I would be glad to give him my opinion, but I would not like to give it authoritatively as Minister of Agriculture.
That is the gentleman I am asking.	-
The Minister of Agriculture ?
Yes.

There are a great many methods of tying up cattle, some of which may be found more convenient in one barn than in another. There are certain things which are required to be, considered in tying up cattle and if the results desired are obtained by tying them by one method in one barn they may not be obtained by tying them by that method in another barn. As a matter of fact I am reconstructing my own stables on my farm, and while there is one method of tying up animals which I think the best, it is not convenient Mr. FISHER.
to put it in my stables and therefore I have to adopt the; second best method. But that is a matter of private information that does not apply to the general subject.

The hon. minister has taken several minutes to tel! us how pattle should be tied up. I would like if he would devote one minute to answering the question of my hon. friend and say which is the best method.

I cannot answer that in one word, because undep one set of circumstances one method may be better than another method under a different set of circumstances.	.
Mr.'INGRAM. Would the hon. gentleman recommend for milch cows the method known as stanchion tying ?
I have put swing stanchions in my own barn.
That is where the head of the cow is placed between two posts and the cow can work 'its head up and dowry, but not sideways.

I said swing stanchions and not fixed posts. These stanchions are madq of two uprights with cross-pieces at the top and bottom. The top is fastened with a little chain with a bar at the top and bottom and a chain below. The result is that the stanchion plays fast and loose and the animal can put its head wherever it likes.
Supposing that at night the milch cow is asleep
Oh.

I am getting down to practical farming. The hon. gentleman used the term of swing stanchion. When the much cow is sleeping, can she sleep as nature intended when a stanchion such as he has described is used ?
Yes.
Will the hon. minister tell us really how nature intended the cow to sleep ?
If the hon. gentleman had watched milch cows sleeping as often as 1 have, he would know without any difficulty.
I am bound to say that there are a good many who do not know.
I have seen them often. They sleep just the same as human beings. Some sleep in one position and some in another.

That may be very satisfactory for the minister, but for practical farmers it is very unsatisfactory. I suppose

we will admit that to have milch cows produce the best possible results, you must, in the matter of rest, adopt such a method as will allow them as nearly as possible to conform to the conditions of nature. If the animals are compelled to occupy positions which are unnatural they will hot produce such good results. This is a serious matter as regards milch cows. It is a very serious matter, and I want to point out to those hon. .gentlemen who think they are farmers, but who are not practical farmers, that by reason of the use of vertical stanchions, which do not allow the milch cow to sleep or rest as nature intended, the cow does not produce the same as she would if she were left to rest as nature intended. I was expecting to hear from the hon. minister that in the matter of these upright stanchions he would not, as Minister of Agriculture, recommend such a mode of tying milch cows. I have listened to some very able lectures, and I confess that the ablest lecture on milch cows I ever listened to was by a lady, who advanced the theory that you should apply the same rule to dumb animals that you apply to human beings, and treat them with the same kindness. That lady came from Wisconsin, and she knew more about dairying than any half dozen of the so-called professors I hear going around the country.

According to the Auditor General's Report, Page D-36, you have expended $59,287.60, less proceeds of sale of 61 steers, amounting to $4,082, leaving a balance of $55,205.60. Does that show a loss of that amount on your operations ?

No ; we buy steers and fatten them for experiment and sell them again. The purchase price goes against the expenditure, and the selling price goes in as an off set to the general expenses of the farm. The money from the sale of crops, fruit, &c., goes into the consolidated revenue account. In round numbers, there are generally sales of $5,000 or $6,000 from the Central Experimental Farm of various products, which do not appear in this account. The suggestion that this is a balance against tire farm is not correct, but even if it were we do not pretend that the sales from the farm cover the expenditure. The expenditure is for the purpose of carrying on experiments, and not for raising crops or fattening animals to sell. Some of these steers were fattened for experiments by various methods and sold in the spring, whereas, if we tried to make money out of them as an ordinary farmer would, fatten them off toy what we considered the best method and probably make more profit.
Well, that is the loss, including the cost of experiment ?

No ; there is included in that $55,000 the salary of the director, of the scientific staff, the work of distribution of bulletins, the distribution of seed, the care of the arboretum, the care of the grounds and buildings, and all that kind of thing.

One would expect that there would be some return from the poultry business, for instance. Poultry can only be raised for two purposes-for sale as food or for the eggs the hens lay. For last year we have a cost of $1,588 for, poultry and a return of $322. The farmer who would not be able to make a better showing would soon reach the poor-house.

The expense of the poultry division includes the salary of Mr. Gilbert who attends to the poultry, and who spends a great deal of his time travelling about the country and addressing public meetings on poultry matters. It also in-eludes the cost of experimental work, such as the comparing of different breeds and ascertaining the results.

The keeping of fowls is not like the care of an experimental plot from which very little return would be expected. One would suppose that the poultry would be kept in such a way as to show what kind of a return a farmer would have from the work.

There are certain expenses which apply to all the farms. At the end of the farm report of last year will be found a statement of expenditure on Dominion experimental farms for the year. The total expenditure is stated in the Auditor General's Report to be $55,205.

In that ease the total salaries of the officers are charged to the Central Farm ; but though they reside here, a. good deal of their correspondence and distribution and other work is divided among the different farms.

speechtext: Am I to understand from the hon. gentleman that the statement which he has just read from his report is a correct statement of the total expenditure in connection with the farm for the year 1902-3 ?
That is the statement my official gives, and I suppose it is correct. It has been audited by the Auditor General.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I will give the hon. gentleman a statement from the Auditor General's Report, and I wiy ask him and his officers to contradict it if they can. ' What the hon. gentleman says is taken from the Auditor General's Report is correct so far as it goes ; but I have given the hon. gentleman a statement in regard to the division of certain work among the different farms.

I am informed by the director that that is not the case.

These are all detailed in the accounts rendered by the Auditor GeneraJ and passed by him.

speechtext: They are certified by the minister, I suppose, or by the accountant of his department, and the Auditor General has to pass them, no matter whether they represent tips to the waiters, or drinks at the bar, or anything else.
That is not the way the Auditor' General generally does. When) an expenditure is made of the exact nature of which he is not advised or does not approve he generally protests.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The next item is exhibi-ions, $692.98, which includes an item of wages detailed of $388.81. The next item is telegrams and telephones, $144.06. Then office help, &c., $4,543.71 which includes salaries and wages detailed of $4,395.06. Then comes printing and stationery, $826.68. Then newspapers and periodicals, $109.09. Then seeds, grain, trees, &c., $446.44. Horticultural department, $5,102.92 ; distribution of seed grain, trees, &c., $4,562.56 ; seed testing and care of greenhouses, $1,691.39 ; Arboretum, $1,892.06 ; forestry department and care of grounds, $1,335.81 ; live stock, $1,496.08 ; farm work, $5,082.35; draining, $1,958.06 ; implements, tools, hardware and supplies, $708.67; blacksmithing and harness supplies, $379.54 ; manure and fertilizers, $310.42 ; dairy department, $715.27; poultry department, $1,773.45 ; bee supplies $218.47 ; contingencies, $128.06 ; division of cereal breeding and experimental, $2,805.47; feed for stock, $930.44; museum, $2.50 ; care of stock. $3,087.45 ; roadmaking and drawing gravel, $116.81 ; steers for feeding experiments, $2,787.85. These items make a total of $59,287.60. Now, will the hon. gentleman tell me how the expenditure in connection with the farm, taking the items I have given as quoted from the Auditor General's Report and the salaries and wages included in which are summarized at page D-37 showing an amount of $44,478.28, agree with his statement. It is true the hon. minister figures the wages and salaries out pretty nearly, but still there is a discrepancy of about $400, because the amount he gives is $44,104,36 as against $44,478.28. Between his statement and that of the Auditor General there is $300 or $400 of a discrepancy. The Auditor General says here that the total expense in connection with this farm is $59,287, yet the hon. gentleman tells the farmers by this report that the experimental farm at Ottawa only costs $44,000. Now by' what sy'stem of book-keeping can the hon. gentleman contradict the statement of the Auditor General ? I have given every detail from his report, every expenditure ; let the hon. gentleman bring down a statement if he can that will contradict that. I say that the loss to this country last year was $62,228.52 as against a loss in the last year of the Conservative administration of $36,420.57, dealing with every item in the same way, when the work was done just as efficiently as the work is being done by the hon. gentleman to-day.

I do not think it is necessary to go over the figures again. The hon. gentleman has again deliberately included in the one statement the whole of the salaries of the officials, and applied it to the Central Experimental Farm in the statement of the Auditor General's Report. In the other statement the whole of these salaries are not charged to the central farm, only a portion of them. That is the whole difference, and I have explained it over and over again. I cannot bring down any statement other than is shown by these figures here. They are the figures of the Auditor General's Report in both cases.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Do they agree ?

The sum total on page 37 is not the same total, the details are not the same, the items are not the same, but because the totals are nearly the same the hon. gentleman has jumped to the conclusion that they ought to be the same. The Auditor General will have to cook the accounts to make them the same. The one includes the whole salaries charged to the central farm ; the other includes only a portion of the salaries, but includes a lot of other things which, in the aggregate, nearly makes up the difference in salaries ; and because they nearly make up the difference the hon. gentleman jumps to the conclusion

that an attempt has been made to make them the same.
The hon. gentleman says that the total of $44,478-28 contains different items than those that are contained at the foot of that page and on the head of the fallowing page.

No, I say they contain totally different items from those on page 429. In that case the $44,478 are for salaries and nothing else ; in the other case the total is $44,104.36, which contains a portion of the salaries which are fairly chargeable to the central farm, and also all the other expenses fairly chargeable to the central farm. Because the figures are so nearly the same the hon. gentleman jumps to the conclusion that they are actually the same, whereas they are totally different.

Even supposing the item with regard to the salaries of these officials is correct and is distributed as the minister states over the different farms in the country, that explanation would not apply to the item of wages. Even allowing' his statement to be correct that in his own report of the experimental farm, the item of salaries of officers is distributed in the proportion that ire thinks is just
That the Auditor General thinks is just.

Whoever makes up the items-distributing that among the various experimental farms, still that explanation would not apply to the item of wages. Now, the item of wages, which the Auditor General. puts down to the central farm at Ottawa, amounts to $21,181.99 ; whereas the amount of wages that the hon. gentleman debits to the central farm amounts to only $9,900. Now, surely such a discrepancy as that merits more explanation than we have had. I cannot understand how the Auditor General debits the central farm with $21,000 in wages, while the minister only debits it with about $10,000.

If the hon. gentlema will turn to page 429 of the experiments farms report he will find the followin charges :
Salaries of officers engaged in the 'general work otf the farms, proportion chargeable to the Central
Farm	51,792 49
Wages, farm work, including experimental work yvith grain and other farm crops : also salaries of officers
in charge	 6,840 54
Wages, care of stock	 3,087 45
Chemical division, proportion chargeable to the Central Farm	1,412 90
Botanical and entomological division, proportion chargeable to the Central
Farm	 1,442 56
Horticultural division, including salary
of officer in charge	 5,110 92 '

Poultry division, including all supplies ;
also salary of officer in charge...$1,992 04
Forestry division and care of grounds.. 1,335 81
And so on. These are the divisions in eluding the wages spent in each. The $21,000 odd off wages shown in the Auditor General's Report includes the care of farm stock and the expenditure for wages in the horticultural division, the chemical division and so on as shown in the farm report. The items are divided up on a different plan and therefore it is almost impossible unless you have the details of the whole work to be able to compare them.

I think the mode which the hon. gentleman has adopted in his report of explaining these expenditures to the country is one calculated to deceive the people. When you find in a detailed report such as this is supposed to be two items, one referring to wages for the caring of stock, and another to wages relating to the farm work, you naturally conclude that these are the only wages which are paid at the Central Experimental Farm. If these other items include wages it is only a reasonable request on the part of the members of this committee that the' amount spent in wages, whether in the care of stock, or farm work, or in the botanical and entomological division, should be credited to the word ' wages ' and then we could understand what was meant. It is absolutely impossible for any one to get a clear understanding of the cost of these various services from this report.

The hon. gentleman may be right in his judgment that this is not the proper form of these accounts, but'with the exception that they have been somewhat amplified in later years and more detailed, these accounts in the report have been practically the same ever since the farm reports have been issued. It may be an incorrect system, but it is the way in which these farm accounts have been made up for the report to show the expenditure of the farms ever since the inception of the farm system.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Would the hon. minister tell the committee what he pays to the superintendent of the farms at Brandon, Indian Head, Agassiz and Nappan ?
$1,500 a year apiece.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Then the hon. gentleman tells us that the balance over and above the $44,000 of expenditure that he shows in his report at page 429 and which is chargeable to the other experimental farms, has been divided. If he will turn over the page in his report he will find the following charge:
Salary of superintendent, including proportion of salaries for general work, Ottawa, $2,545.62.
And the same for the farms at Brandon, Indian Head and Agassiz. Deducting $1,500

that leaves $1,000 that they have paid as their proportion of the wages paid by the experimental farm, which would amount to
,j*0. The Auditor General in his report at page D-36 states that the cost of these farms has been $59,227. Will the hon. minister explain to me where the difference has gone ?
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the details of that difference.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said that the difference is made up in the wages that are charged to the other farms. He is misleading the people, because there is only $1,000 charged there.
That would not make up the difference.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, it does not make it up. The hon. gentleman should be able to give us a 'statement explaining that.
I will try to give the information.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
He has told the farmers that it only costs $44,000 when the amount is $69,000, according to the details which are given in the Auditor General's Report. My hon. friend says that he has charged that to the other farms, but when we take up his report in regard to the other farms he only charges $1,045 as their proportion of the expenses at Ottawa. So, there is a discrepancy of $20,000 to be accounted for. We must know where that has gone.
Mr. SPROUT,E. I think it would be better for the hon. minister to allow this item to stand and bring down a statement giving that information.

I will be quite ready to do so, and if hon. gentlemen opposite will say wnat they would like in the way of information I will try to get it. I do not wish to force the item through without full information. I am quite satisfied that the information is get-at-able and will prove perfectly satisfactory to the committee. It is the right of the House to have all the informatioh that hon gentlemen have asked for and I would be only too glad to bring it down. I know what my hon. friend from South Leeds wants, I know what my hon. friend from East Elgin has asked for, but if there is any other information that is desired I will be glad to bring it down. I take it for granted that hon. gentlemen do not wish to waste the time of the House, that they do not wish to obstruct. Of course I could not for a moment think that they would do that, because at this late date of the session I take it that they must be anxious to put the work through.

I can assure the hon. gentleman we have no desire to obstruct the work. We only wish to get the information
so that it may be understandable and that it may be presented to the country in such a form that the country will understand it as well.

I think the hon. minister has shown a desire to furnish the committee with all the information that he can, but he evidently could not give uB the information which we desired in reference to some of these items.
I coufd not go into the details of the accounts on the spur of the moment.

I would like the hon. gentleman to explain the item at the bottom of page I)-37 of the Auditor General's Report :
Salaries, general, $5,974.96.
I will try to find that out.
Some time ago I asked the hon. gentleman for information about the number of members of the agricultural societies of the Northwest.
I have sent to the Northwest to get the details. I think the information has arrived by this time, but I will ask my deputy minister. As soon as it arrives I will give it to my hon. friend.
Is there any other revenue from the experimental farm except from the sale of the stock ? I see you keep bees ; what do you do with the honey ?
We sell honey, and eggs, and fruit; the farm crops are all fed on the farm. The details of the sales are in the Auditor General's Report.

The minister understands that we want an account of the total expenditure on the experimental farm here in the various lines, and as well, the revenue from that farm on account of the sales. That will apply to all the farms. We want the expenditure on the various farms, taking into account the proportion that belongs to each of them, because I understand the minister to say that a certain portion of what should be charged to the other farms is included in the expenditure of the central farm here.
That appears in the Auditor General's Report.
We would like to have that charged to each of the farms in every line, public works or any other line.

The details of the public works expenditure are given exactly on tha different farms. If we build a barn at Agassiz, for instance, it is taken out of that $10,000. The details are all in the Auditor General's Report, but of course the hon. gentleman does not wish himself to look it up, and I will have to get one of the officials

to look it up and hand it to him. Now, first of all, I understand he wants an explanation of what is called the discrepancy between the statement at the end of the farm report and the statement in the Auditor General's Report; and, in the second place, he wants the actual statement of the expenditure on the central farm here for the work of the central farm, not including these salaries of officers which are for the whole system.
The proportion properly charged to this central farm.

Exactly. He wants it divided up on the principle which is applied in this statement at the end of the farm report. That is the principle on which that statement is made, and I venture to say that statement will be found to be absolutely correct. The only difficulty at present is that I do not quite see where the whole of the difference between that and the statement in the Auditor General's Report comes in. 1 thought it was almost all due to the difference in regard to the amount of salaries charged, but if the figures of the member for Leeds are correct and cover the whole, that cannot be the only difference. I will find out if there is any other difference. It there is anything I have not covered, I should be only too glad to be reminded.
And the aggregate of the revenue derived from the different farms.
Yes.
When the superintendent of the experimental farm was before the Agricultural Committee I gave notice that I intended to ask as to the revenue and expenditure on each of the farms separately
The total revenue and the total expenditure ?
Yes. The director, not having come before the committee again, we thought this was the best place to ask for that information.

Undoubtedly. If that is all the information th/e hon. gentleman wants, I will try to bring it down. If hon. gentlemen are satisfied with it, I suppose they will allow the item to pass after the usual fair discussion on the next occasion. I move that the committee rise.
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In accordance with the statement orf the premier early in the day, I beg to lay on the table the remainder of the correspondence relating to the removal of Lord Dun-donald.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That will be printed with the other ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I suppose the previous order for printing will cover it.
I move the ; djournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will proceed with supply, the estimates being those of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Postmaster General, and perhaps Customs. I am not quite sure as to their order, but probably we may begin with Marine and Fisheries.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Friday, June 17, 1904.
